subject: Cloud Computing
title: Google's Global Network
description: Learn Google's Global Network in one minute.

hook.text: Google owns one of the largest private networks on Earth — over 100,000 miles of fiber-optic cable.

buildup.text: This network connects Google's data centers at speeds most companies could never achieve.

discovery.text: GCP customers ride this network. Their traffic stays on Google's private fiber, avoiding public internet congestion.

twist.text: Google's network advantage is hard to replicate. Laying undersea cables costs hundreds of millions per line.

climax.text: Network performance is an invisible differentiator. Users don't see it, but their apps feel it.

punchline.text: Google's secret weapon is buried under the ocean.

quiz.question: How does Google's private network benefit GCP customers?
options: Traffic stays on Google's fast private fiber, avoiding public internet congestion
Customers get free internet access at home through Google's cables
The network encrypts data automatically without any customer configuration

details.summary: Google operates one of the world's largest private networks, with subsea cables spanning oceans and fiber connecting data centers across continents. This network provides lower latency and higher throughput between regions than competitors who rely more on the public internet.
details.whyItMatters: Google's network advantage translates to faster, more reliable connections between regions. For globally distributed applications, Google's network can provide measurably better performance.
takeaways: Google owns subsea cables and global fiber infrastructure
Traffic enters Google's network at the nearest edge and stays private

faq.question: How does Google's network differ from competitors?
faq.answer: Google routes traffic onto its private network at the city closest to the user, keeping it on Google infrastructure for most of the journey. Competitors often route traffic through the public internet for longer portions. This difference is measurable in latency and reliability.

faq.question: Does Google own undersea cables?
faq.answer: Yes. Google has invested in multiple subsea cable systems including Dunant (US-Europe), Equiano (Europe-Africa), and Grace Hopper (US-UK-Spain). These privately owned cables give Google control over international bandwidth capacity and routing.
